subdomainName: Design and Validate Assessment, Test, and Audit Strategies
topicName: Internal vs. External vs. Third-Party Assessments
title: First-, second- and third-party assessments
prompt: Contrast first-, second- and third-party assessments by who performs them and how independent they are.
answerSummary: First-party: internal staff assess their own organization. Second-party: a customer or partner assesses a supplier. Third-party: an independent external auditor; most objective and used for certifications and regulatory attestations.
examTrapWarning: When a question asks for the most objective or credible assurance for external stakeholders, choose the independent third-party audit.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Independence rises from first to third party.

columns.label: Second-party
points: Performed by a customer or partner

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Design and Validate Assessment, Test, and Audit Strategies
title: Before any penetration test starts
prompt: A team lead wants to start scanning and exploiting production systems tonight to "see what we find". What must happen first?
answerSummary: Get written authorization from senior management (the system owner) and agree rules of engagement: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts, data handling and how to stop the test.
examTrapWarning: Without written permission, a penetration test is indistinguishable from an attack and may be illegal. Verbal approval from IT is not enough.

heuristicData.technicalReflexTrap: Start the scan right away because the team has admin credentials and good intentions.
heuristicData.managerAction: Obtain signed management authorization and a rules-of-engagement document defining scope, schedule, methods, contacts and emergency stop procedures before any active testing.
heuristicData.governingPrinciple: Testing requires documented management approval; scope and rules of engagement protect the organization and the testers.

references.section: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

title: Vulnerability scan vs. penetration test
prompt: Contrast a vulnerability scan with a penetration test.
answerSummary: A vulnerability scan is automated and broad; it identifies potential weaknesses with low impact and can run often. A penetration test is human-driven; it tries to exploit weaknesses to prove real business impact, needs explicit authorization and carries operational risk.
examTrapWarning: A scan only reports possible vulnerabilities (with false positives). Proving exploitability and impact requires a pen test.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

title: Black-box vs. gray-box vs. white-box testing
prompt: Contrast tester knowledge in black-, gray- and white-box tests.
answerSummary: Black box (zero knowledge): tester starts like an outsider; most realistic for external attackers, slowest. Gray box (partial knowledge): some details such as user credentials; simulates an insider or compromised user. White box (full knowledge): tester has source code, diagrams and credentials; most thorough per hour.
examTrapWarning: For thorough coverage within limited time, white box. For realism of an external attacker, black box.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: More knowledge = more coverage, less realism.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

title: Penetration test phases (NIST SP 800-115)
prompt: Put the four penetration testing phases in order.
answerSummary: Planning → Discovery → Attack → Reporting. Discovery and attack loop as new access reveals more targets.
examTrapWarning: Planning (including authorization and rules of engagement) always comes first; reporting includes clean-up and remediation guidance.

steps.label: Planning
steps.detail: Set scope, rules of engagement, authorization and goals.

steps.label: Attack
steps.detail: Gain access, escalate privileges, pivot; loops back to discovery.

steps.label: Reporting
steps.detail: Document findings, risk and remediation; clean up artifacts.

references.section: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

topicName: SAST, DAST, IAST, SCA, Fuzzing, Code Review
title: SAST vs. DAST vs. IAST vs. SCA vs. fuzzing
prompt: Match each application testing technique to what it examines and when.
answerSummary: SAST: static analysis of source or binaries without running them (white box, early). DAST: tests a running application from outside (black box). IAST: instruments the running app to watch code paths during tests. SCA: inventories open-source components and known CVEs. Fuzzing: feeds malformed or random input to find crashes.
examTrapWarning: SAST cannot find runtime configuration issues; DAST cannot point to the exact line of code. Vulnerable third-party libraries are found with SCA.

rows: Behavior under malformed input (mutation or generation)

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)
ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: SAST, DAST, IAST, SCA, Fuzzing, Code Review
title: Fagan inspection steps
prompt: Put the six steps of a Fagan code inspection in order.
answerSummary: Planning → Overview → Preparation → Inspection → Rework → Follow-up.
mnemonic: Please Order Pizza In Real Fast.
examTrapWarning: Fagan inspection is the most formal code review; defects found in inspection are fixed in rework and verified in follow-up.

steps.label: Overview
steps.detail: Author explains the code and its context.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: Account Management Reviews, KPIs/KRIs, Backup Verification
title: KPI vs. KRI
prompt: Distinguish key performance indicators from key risk indicators.
answerSummary: KPIs measure how well a process or control is performing (for example patch compliance rate). KRIs are forward-looking signals that risk is rising toward appetite thresholds (for example number of unpatched critical systems exposed to the internet).
examTrapWarning: A metric with a threshold that triggers escalation when risk exceeds appetite is a KRI.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: KPI looks back at performance; KRI warns of rising risk.

columns.label: KPI
points: How well a process meets its goal
Example: % of systems patched within SLA

columns.label: KRI
points: Early warning that risk is increasing
Forward-looking, tied to risk appetite thresholds
Example: count of critical vulns past due

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: Account Management Reviews, KPIs/KRIs, Backup Verification
title: Synthetic transactions vs. real user monitoring
prompt: Contrast synthetic (active) monitoring and real user (passive) monitoring.
answerSummary: Synthetic monitoring runs scripted transactions on a schedule to test availability and function, even with no users online. Real user monitoring passively records actual user sessions to show real performance and errors.
examTrapWarning: To detect a failure before customers notice (for example at 3 a.m.), use synthetic transactions.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Synthetic = scripted probes; RUM = real traffic.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Analyze Test Output and Generate Report
topicName: False Positives vs. False Negatives, CVSS Prioritization
title: False positives vs. false negatives
prompt: Contrast false positives and false negatives in scanning and detection, and say which is more dangerous.
answerSummary: A false positive is an alert for something that is not a real issue; it wastes time and causes alert fatigue. A false negative is a real vulnerability or attack that goes undetected; it is more dangerous because nobody responds.
examTrapWarning: Tuning to remove all false positives can raise false negatives. The dangerous error is the silent one.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: False negatives are the dangerous silence.

columns.label: False positive
points: Reports an issue that is not real

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Analyze Test Output and Generate Report
topicName: False Positives vs. False Negatives, CVSS Prioritization
title: CVSS metric groups
prompt: List the CVSS metric groups and what each captures.
answerSummary: Base: intrinsic severity that does not change. Temporal (v3.1) / Threat (v4.0): factors that change over time such as exploit maturity. Environmental: adjusts for the organization's own system importance and controls. CVSS v4.0 also adds optional Supplemental metrics.
examTrapWarning: Prioritize with environmental context: a CVSS 9.8 on an isolated lab box may matter less than a 7.5 on an internet-facing payment server.

rows: Intrinsic characteristics: attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact
Changes over time, e.g., exploit code maturity
Your environment: asset criticality and mitigating controls
Extra context such as safety and automatable; does not change the score

references.source: FIRST CVSS v3.1 and v4.0 Specifications

topicName: SOC 1 (Type I/II), SOC 2 (Type I/II), SOC 3, ISO 27001 Audits
title: SOC 1 vs. SOC 2 vs. SOC 3
prompt: Compare SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3 reports by focus and audience.
answerSummary: SOC 1: controls relevant to financial reporting (ICFR), for the customer's auditors. SOC 2: controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security required; availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy optional), detailed and shared under NDA. SOC 3: a general-use summary of SOC 2 suitable for the public.
examTrapWarning: To evaluate a cloud provider's security controls in detail, ask for a SOC 2 Type II, not SOC 1 (financial) or SOC 3 (public summary).

rows: User entities and their financial auditors
Trust Services Criteria: security (required), availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy
Restricted: customers and prospects under NDA
Summary of SOC 2 results without control details

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: SOC 1 (Type I/II), SOC 2 (Type I/II), SOC 3, ISO 27001 Audits
title: SOC Type I vs. Type II
prompt: Contrast SOC Type I and Type II reports.
answerSummary: Type I evaluates the design of controls at a single point in time. Type II evaluates design and operating effectiveness over a period, typically 6–12 months, so it gives more assurance.
mnemonic: Type I = one Instant. Type II = over Time.
examTrapWarning: A Type I says controls look right on paper on one day; only Type II shows they actually worked over time.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Type II is the one that proves controls operated.
